newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: USTR Barshefsky says infotech deal 'already there'.
newsitem.headline: USTR Barshefsky says infotech deal 'already there'.

text.p: Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said on Friday there was no question that an agreement to eliminate tariffs in the fast-growing information technology market by 2000 would be implemented next year.

"Criterion number one -- do we have approximately 90 percent of trade covered? We are already there," she told a news conference on the final day of the week-long World Trade Organisation (WTO) meeting in Singapore.
Inclusion of 90 percent of the trade was the key hurdle set by the European Union (EU) and United States for implementation of the information technology agreement (ITA).
Barshefky said 28 countries, representing 84 percent of global trade in information technology products, had already signed the agreement to eliminate tariffs in the sector.
With another six countries committed to signing, total volume coverage of the information technology agreement (ITA) would exceed 90 percent, she said.
The WTO estimates world exports of information technology products totalled around $600 billion in 1995. Analysts say the sector is growing by at least 15 percent annually.
Barshefsky told the news conference initially that another three countries were ready to sign up, but after consulting officials she corrected the figure to six.
She read a list of the 28 countries that had already signed up to the ITA.
"It is 28 countries representing 84 percent of global trade in IT products," she said.
She said the WTO secretariat had projected that 94 percent of trade in information technology products could be covered by the deal.
Barshefsky said the ITA agreement laid out a timetable for tariff cuts in four stages up to the year 2000.
But she said the agreement allowed countries to remove tariffs at a faster pace if they wished.
"It would be our hope that at a minimum we (the United States) and the European Union would accelerate our tariff cuts. "We would not wait until the year 2000 to go to zero."
European officials had earlier said final agreement on an ITA still depended on countries representing about 90 percent of world trade in information technology joining the pact by March 15, 1997.
They said the ITA, reached after four days of intense, round-the-clock talks, marked the most far-reaching agreement ever towards free trade in a single sector.
It should slash prices not only on high-technology but on goods from cars to copiers to washing machines.

The deal covers the bulk of industrial information technology products, as well as digital photocopiers and capacitors -- circuits used in electronic equipment-- while excluding consumer electronics and audio materials.
EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan earlier called the ITA "a huge advance for the world economy". He said: "It will be good for the IT industry, and will act as a catalyst for industrial growth."

The 28 countries that have signed up include the 15 EU members and the United States. The others are Australia, Canada, Hong Kong, Iceland, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Norway, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan and Turkey.
